description_full: Albany International Corp., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the machine clothing and engineered composites businesses in the United States, Switzerland, France, Brazil, China, Mexico, Germany, and internationally. The company operates through two segments: Machine Clothing (MC) and Albany Engineered Composites (AEC). The MC segment designs, manufactures, and markets paper machine clothing for use in the manufacturing of papers, paperboard, tissues, towels, pulps, building products, tannery, and textiles, as well as nonwovens, fiber cement, and several other industrial applications. This segment offers paper machine clothing forming, pressing, and drying fabrics, as well as processing belts; and engineered fabrics. Its AEC segment 3D-woven and injected composite components for aircraft engines composite airframe and engine components for military and commercial aircraft. The company sells its products to commercial and defense markets, space-launch vehicles and the emerging advanced air mobility market, as well as to customer end-users. Albany International Corp. was incorporated in 1895 and is headquartered in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

financial_summary: Albany International Corporatio is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.9B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 38%.
The business throws off $83M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
Accruals are elevated at -12.2% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin -1.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 11.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
